column2: Having imposed the counter-subject and describing it as non-different from it — that is Mohopama of the subject, the Bhrantimat statement (mistaken identity).
When the truth of both possessors is not settled, Samshaya-upama (doubt); when the subject, having been doubted, is determined, Nishchaya-upama.
Vakyartha-upama arises by the sentence-meaning itself, from the comparison; from comparison with oneself, Atishayini-upama through common property.
What is the subject of another is held the simile of that other; if it goes on from one to the next, then it is Gagana-upama.
Praise, blame, invented, similar and slightly similar — the simile is to be known as fivefold at first.
When the nature of the subject is presented through the standard of comparison, seeing the equality of qualities, they know it as Rupaka (metaphor).
Simile with the difference concealed is Rupaka; Sahokti is statement of things of like property together by co-presence.
Arthantaranyasa would be by likeness with a following (statement); the situation of a sentient and of another presented otherwise,
where one thinks otherwise, they call it Utpreksha. Description of a thing's property exceeding the limits of the world
is called Atishaya, twofold: possible and impossible. Where the lack of qualities, kind, action and the like is shown
only for the sake of seeing distinction, that is called Visheshokti. By negation of a well-known cause, where some other cause
or natural state is to be conceived, that is Vibhavana. Bringing into agreement by reasoning two things that do not agree,
by being preceded by contradiction is remembered as Virodha. A reason becomes the proof of the matter to be established;
it arises as twofold: Karaka (causative) and Jnapaka (indicative). The one called Karaka proceeds before and after the birth of the effect;
it is famed as "poorva-shesha" of those very two distinctions; by cause-and-effect relation, by nature, or by the restrictor;
the division called Jnapaka is by seeing the flood of a river and the like; the rule of invariable concomitance is from seeing invariable concomitance.
Manifestness is revelation; Shruti and Akshepa too. Its two divisions: Shruti there is a word giving over its own meaning,
it would be occasional and technical, twofold only. Convention is "terminology" (paribhasha), hence it is Paribhashiki;
and Mukhya and Aupacharika — each twofold. Aupacharika is a word that, with its own denotation failing, denotes a non-primary meaning
through some ground; that is Lakshanika and Gauni, by connection of indication and quality.
The understanding inseparable from the denoted is called Lakshana (indication): by relation with the denoted, nearness, inherence,
opposition and action-connection, Lakshana is held fivefold; Gauni is endless by endlessness of qualities, in the wish to express that.
Another's property elsewhere, in accordance with the limits of the world, is properly placed — that is here remembered as Samadhi.
A meaning not obtainable from the text but shining in the mind — that is Akshepa and Dhvani; and it is suggested by Dhvani.
Where meaning by word or meaning, having itself gained it — a special thing, as if prohibition of the desired, in the wish to say,
they call Akshepa; here Stuta is this praise again: praise of another thing irrelevant to the context;
where the meaning said is not understood, an equal qualifier — that is Samasokti told by the wise for brevity of sense.
Apahnuti conceals and suggests something of another meaning; Paryayokta is what is said in another way; of these one alone is thus named Dhvani.
Absence of harsh letters, mostly (soft) words, tenderness; with plain words, generosity and praiseworthy qualifiers —
Ojas is abundance of compounds; this is the life of verse and the rest. From Brahma to a blade of grass, manliness is by Ojas alone;
the meaning that, by whatever word it is said of a thing, brings out excellence is called a "quality" (guna).
Sweetness, arrangement (sambidhana), softness, generosity, maturity (praudhi) and conventionality — these six divisions shine.
From anger, envy, appearance and depth, sweetness; entry into steadiness; sambidhana is the apparatus for accomplishing the needed;
where distinguished arrangement free of hardness and the like, putting it down, tenderness shines — that is Komalata;
it is seen where there is mark of operating on gross marks: the quality's generosity, excess of fineness of intention;
toward the intended, the arguments that accomplish its fulfillment, full of reasons, are declared maturity and immaturity;
of the independent and the dependent, by union of outer and inner agreement — the learning of meaning there is Samayikata (conventionality).
One benefiting both word and meaning is remembered as having the quality of both. Its Prasada, Saubhagya, in order Prashastata,
Paka, Raga — thus sixfold expansion by the wise. Use of well-known meaning words is sung as Prasada;
some quality with excellence, understood when it is stated — that the wise call Saubhagya, generosity;
by order without enumeration the common is directed; even of a dreadful thing, at the time of description,
description with a non-dreadful word is Prashastata. Some high ripening is called Paka;
by the differences of grape, coconut and water ripening it is fourfold; sweetness at the beginning and end — that is grape-ripening.
A special thing by poetic wish is sung as Raga; accompanied by practice it persists as natural radiance;
turmeric-colored, safflower-colored, and indigo-colored — Raga is threefold. The distinctive is to be known as what is within the range of its own marks.
A fault is general and specific; the latter is of meaning, twofold. Reproach of many parts is remembered as general;
failure of action and agent, faulty juncture, repetition, and disconnected relation — five are held general;
non-action, failure of action, fallen agency again; absence of agent and the like: faulty juncture is defect of sandhi;
the juncture is either lost or contradictory, twofold; contradictoriness of juncture from harsh foot or arrival of another meaning;
repetition is statement by frequency, twofold; repetition of meaning and of word; repetition of meaning too is twofold;
by the word used and by another word; in word-repetition the word is repeated, not the speakable;
disconnected relation is good relation through intervening, by expression of another relation or arisen from another relation;
even in absence of those two, by intervention — threefold; again twofold according to intervening word or sentence;
the speakable, by being in need of meaning, twofold: of word and of sentence; divided into earlier-explained speakable and to-be-explained.
Causing contradiction to the desired is incapacity of the reason: unestablished, contradictory, inconclusive,
counter-balanced, past-time, mixed; in the party, in the similar, not existing; in the dissimilar existing — that.
In poems, for those in assemblies there would be no grating; eleven kinds of meaninglessness are not faulted in the hard-to-do (dushkara);
it pains those who know faults; hidden meaning is not a fault in the difficult; vulgarity does not distress by the fame of world and scripture.
There is a mark by failure of action through supplying an action; fallen agency by the force of implication supplies the agent;
in the unseparable (pragrihya) it is not taken; a defect is not by lost juncture; faulty juncture by harsh reading is not unfortunate in hard speech and the like.
In alliteration word-repetition and disconnected relation are good; no fault in gathering of meaning; not stained by inversions and the like.
Where case-endings, names and genders do not distress the wise, the number's difference between the standard and the subject
is good: one with many, many with many. The usage of poets is called Samaya (convention).
It is general and special, twofold like dharma. By lack of dispute among the Siddhantins and poets,
what is well established is held the general convention; by which all Siddhantins proceed without fault,
or only some; by that it is twofold. A cut-established, another, is from the error of some, as:
logical knowledge of some sage; momentariness for some; consciousness of elements for some; clarity of knowledge for some;
the many-sidedness of the Arhat; the view of Shaiva, Vaishnava, Shakta and Saura Siddhantins;
Brahman is the cause of the world; the Sankhyas' with Pradhana. In this world of Sarasvati, moving mutually,
they bind, seeing across, what is by the distinguished. From acceptance even of the false, from non-acceptance of the true only,
for that which is divided this twofoldness is sung. What is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge they know as false;
that should be accepted by poets, the shining of knowledge. What alone performs a purposeful action is alone ultimately real;

from ignorance and from knowledge, Brahman alone is ultimately real. Vishnu is the cause of heaven and the rest, having the form of word-ornament; the lower and the higher knowledge — having known it one is freed from existence.
Na is in extracting and in certainty; "ta" is a thief, and a boar's tail; "tha" is in eating, "da" in cutting; "da" is held in bearing and shining;
dha in the Creator and datura; "na" in a multitude, and good-going; "pa" is famed in a grove; "pha" is held in a storm-wind.
